signals.title: @anirudhg192: How Visual Evidence Supports Intelligence Workflows A satellite image may show a ship where a tracking system shows nothing. But that is an
signals.content: How Visual Evidence Supports Intelligence Workflows A satellite image may show a ship where a tracking system shows nothing. But that is an observation, not proof of illegal activity. What matters is how the image is compared with other data. In a 2024 Nature study, Global Fishing Watch researchers analysed satellite imagery alongside billions of vessel positions. They estimated that 72–76% of industrial fishing vessels were not publicly tracked during 2017–2021. Radar detections had to be classified and matched against Automatic Identification System (AIS) signals. Detection also became less reliable for vessels under 25 metres. A visual intelligence workflow has several technical layers. First, the imagery must be prepared. Images are georeferenced, corrected where necessary and aligned with other images. Acquisition time, resolution, sensor type and cloud cover matter. Poor alignment can make ordinary differences in viewing angle or lighting look like changes on the ground. Then comes detection. Optical imagery records reflected light, while synthetic aperture radar (SAR) measures microwave backscatter. SAR works at night and through clouds. Computer vision models can detect vessels or vehicles; segmentation can map roads or floodwater. Change detection highlights what appeared, disappeared or moved between observations. But detection is not identification. A bright radar return might indicate a vessel, but it does not establish its identity or intent. This is where data fusion becomes important: detections are compared with AIS tracks using time, location and plausible movement, alongside maps and older imagery. An unmatched detection calls for review, not an automatic allegation. Another example came after the 2023 Türkiye earthquakes. Copernicus Emergency Management Service used very-high-resolution satellite imagery for rapid damage mapping. By 10 February, 53 maps had been delivered to help assess potentially damaged buildings and roads. These were image-based estimates, not confirmed findings from ground inspections. The difficult part is managing uncertainty. A model's confidence score is not the same as certainty. Image resolution, shadows, false detections, outdated reference data and positioning errors can change the conclusion. Each finding should ideally retain its source, coordinates, timestamp, method and the reason it was flagged. That is what interests me about visual intelligence. The challenge is not just building a model that recognises objects. It is creating an evidence trail that can be checked, questioned and used responsibly. I'd like to connect with researchers, startups and others working on remote sensing, computer vision, geospatial intelligence or visual evidence verification. I'd be interested to hear where these approaches work well and where the biggest practical gaps remain. #VisualIntelligence #GeospatialIntelligence #ComputerVision #OSINT

Images captured on September 18, 2026, show two nearly completed buildings, including a suspected solid-fuel rocket motor casting facility protected by blast-deflection walls. According to FPRI researchers, the expansion could enable Saudi Arabia to manufacture larger ballistic missiles with longer ranges and heavier payloads. However, production of new missile types has not yet been confirmed.
